title: Freezer multisigs use 2-of-N thresholds because halting is fail-safe while changing is not
content:
Across every SkyLink deployment the signing requirement is the same shape: the Ethereum multisig is 2/5 (A.4.2.2.1.2), Solana 2/4 (A.4.2.2.2.3.1.1.2), Avalanche 2/5 (A.4.2.2.3.3.1.1.2), Plasma 2/5 (A.4.2.2.4.3.1.1.2). The absolute threshold never rises with N — two signatures always suffice.

A 2-of-5 threshold would be reckless for a power that could move funds or upgrade code, because it makes capture cheap: compromise two keys and you own the capability. It is defensible here only because of what the capability *is*. A freeze does not move value, does not change logic, and does not authorize anything — it removes a permission. Its worst-case abuse is denial of service on a bridge, which governance can reverse through the ordinary Executive Vote path.

So the design makes the classic emergency-response trade in favour of liveness of the response: false negatives (an exploit proceeding because signers could not be assembled in time) are catastrophic and irreversible, while false positives (an unnecessary freeze) cost users inconvenience. Optimizing threshold downward buys reaction speed at the price of accepting occasional wrongful halts.

The general principle this encodes is worth extracting from the specifics: **thresholds should scale with the irreversibility of the action, not with the sensitivity of the system.** Sky applies a permissive threshold to the stop button and reserves strict process for anything that alters state.
description: Every SkyLink freezer needs only 2 signatures out of 4 or 5. The low bar optimizes for reaction speed against exploits, accepting that a wrongful freeze is recoverable but a slow one is not.
